Hi XXX -- glad you are trying it out.

That problem description, though, is very vague -- in general you will have to quote at least the command and the resulting error in order for someone to help you.

But, you can check:

1. Your working directory (wd), whether you have successfully set R to use the wd (setwd command), and whether or not you can write any files to it ("write permission", I don't know how it works in Windows).

to XXX
Hi XXX,

The Lagrange split probabilities are actually not the same thing as the BioGeoBEARS probabilities, although they will usually be close.  There are a number of different things:

1. The probability of each range at each node (each node is at the top of a branch, except the root node), under the globally-optimum ML parameters.

2. The probability of each each at each "branch bottom" or "corner", under the globally optimum ML parameters

3. The probability of each range at each node, when that range is assumed to be the known true range at that node, and the parameters are re-optimized under that constraint. This is known as locally-optimized ancestral states (compared to global ancestral states, above).

4. The probability of each split scenario, given #3.

This leads us to:
* Python Lagrange reports #4
* C++ Lagrange can report #3 and #4 I believe
* From #4 you can collapse to #3
* BioGeoBEARS gives #1 and #2
* Combining #1 and #2 does not give you #3 / #4 (although it might be correlated)
* To get something like #4 in BioGeoBEARS, you would have to do Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping, and count, for a particular node, how many split scenarios of each type are observed

The difference between global and local ancestral states is discussed in Matzke (2014) and Felsenstein's (2004) book and references therein.

It is extremely common in the literature now to just use/report/plot #1 and #2, so that should be fine, unless someone really cares specifically about the probability of a particular scenario (rather than the average probability of states across all possible scenarios), in which case they should use Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping.

Other things to read:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_joint
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_events

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-validation#BGB_validation
==============
Validation tests of BioGeoBEARS — Introduction
(link to this section)

Here I post some validation examples for BioGeoBEARS.

I have left out comparisons to Lagrange, which are documented in Matzke (2014, Systematic Biology), and which test:

the downpass log-likelihood calculations under the DEC model,
the parameter inferences for d and e, and
the maximum likelihood (ML) optimizer.
Although under the DEC model, the ML log-likelihood and parameter estimates are identical, the ancestral states estimates are not directly comparable between Lagrange and BioGeoBEARS, because:

Lagrange estimated node state/range probabilities under "local optimization", i.e. for every possible ancestral range at every node, Lagrange runs a new ML optimization of the parameters while fixing that range at that node.
BioGeoBEARS estimates ancestral states/ranges under the globally optimum ML model.
Local and global ancestral state/range probabilities will typically be similar but not identical.
==============

Anonymized reply to an issue with NaNs with areas_allowed file

>On Thu, Jan 4, 2018 at 6:36 AM, XXX wrote:
>Hi Nick,
>
>Thanks for posting your suggestion in the google group. Apologies for not posting  the error messges
>
>I have  tried running the codes with the changes you suggested.

>Now i ended up with  the following error messages
>
>Error in calc_loglike_sp(tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state = subtree_tip_relative_probs_of_each_state,  :
>
> Error in calc_uppass_scenario_probs_new2(probs_ancstate, COO_weights_columnar,  :
>
>  STOP ERROR in sample_uppass_split_scenario_given_probs_ancstate()
>

I have attached a Rmarkdown html output for you to have a look.

Looking forward for your suggestions

Hi -- OK, I tried running it.  The problem wasn't with saving, it was NaNs (Not A Number) in the likelihood calcualtion.

You are getting these NaNs because, somewhere in the likelihood calculation, the data are being given 0 likelihood, i.e. 0 probability.  This causes 0/0 errors and other issues.

If the likelihood is 0, this means your data have 0 probability, which is a big problem, since it means the data are impossible under your proposed model!

The problem is the areas_allowed file, it runs fine if that is commented out.  It is quite easy to set up areas_allowed constraints that make your data impossible.  And, in general, the areas_allowed file is of very limited utility -- it is better to manually modify the states_list for any complex scenario.  And, whatever you do, you have to make sure that you don't create impossible scenarios.

See my previous comments on this in various places:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#areas_allowed_matrix2
http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#manual_modify_states
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/biogeobears/7bBNhV904f8/_2eBt6PuAAAJ

...or other searches on the Google Group.

Cheers!

Nick

messages.subject: phylogenies used in BioGeoBEARS should generally be dated...???
messages.subject_clean: phylogenies used in BioGeoBEARS should generally be dated...???
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have been looking through the BioGeoBEARS PhyloWiki and though I was looking for a justification for only presenting the results of the model with the highest log likelihood score (different topic) in manuscripts I stumbled upon this in the Biogeobears Mistakes To Avoid:

"The phylogenies used in BioGeoBEARS should generally be dated. They do not have to be ultrametric, because they might include fossil species/populations (see Fossil data in biogeographical analysis in BioGeoBEARS)...If the user inputs an undated tree (with branch lengths in terms of expected amount of molecular change, for instance), BioGeoBEARS will accept it, and likelihood calculations will be performed, and ancestral states estimated, under these assumptions, without throwing an error. HOWEVER, what is happening here is that BioGeoBEARS is assuming that the highest tip in the rooted tree (as read by APE when APE reads in the Newick file) is at time 0 (the present), and all lower tips in the phylogeny are interpreted as fossils, dated according to the branchlengths below the highest tip at time 0. This makes no difference to the likelihood calculations in an unconstrained, non-time-stratified analysis, so the analysis will run, but it is unclear what the point would be."

But then in the sample input script it says,
"You can use non-ultrametric trees, but BioGeoBEARS will interpret any tips significantly below the  top of the tree as fossils!  This is only a good idea if you actually do have fossils in your tree."

Specific questions:
1) Does this mean that the input tree should be a dated phylogeny such as that produced by BEAST (for example) and created with fossil constraints? That I shouldn't use a RAxML tree and never a species tree (ASTRAL branch lengths are coalescent units and are a direct measure of the amount of discordance in the gene trees)?

2) There aren't any fossils in my phylogeny. I do use fossils as constraints when running dating analyses (BEAST, TreePL) at deeper nodes. Can I therefore just use an ultrametric tree? I should note by main question is to estimate the ancestral range of a a few taxa in a much bigger clade.

Any input on this is greatly appreciated - I don't want to end up in the "mistakes in the literature" section of the biogeobears website! :)

Thanks,
Rebecca

This makes no difference to the likelihood calculations in an unconstrained, non-time-stratified analysis, so the analysis will run, but it is unclear what the point would be."
>

> "You can use non-ultrametric trees, but BioGeoBEARS will interpret any tips significantly below the  top of the tree as fossils!  This is only a good idea if you actually do have fossils in your tree."

> 1) Does this mean that the input tree should be a dated phylogeny such as that produced by BEAST (for example) and created with fossil constraints? That I shouldn't use a RAxML tree

Yes, never a RAxML tree, unless you took some additional steps to transform it to a dated tree (with e.g. r8s).

> and never a species tree (ASTRAL branch lengths are coalescent units and are a direct measure of the amount of discordance in the gene trees)?

A dated species tree is fine, an ultrametric species tree with relative dates is mostly fine (keeping in mind that the dates aren't real, they are some scaling of the true dates), a non-ultrametric species tree would NOT be fine (unless the tips that fail to come up to the present are fossil tips).

> 2) There aren't any fossils in my phylogeny. I do use fossils as constraints when running dating analyses (BEAST, TreePL) at deeper nodes. Can I therefore just use an ultrametric tree? I should note by main question is to estimate the ancestral range of a a few taxa in a much bigger clade.

Yes, typically a dated, ultrametric tree would come from an analysis of molecular data, with the fossils used only as node-date-calibrations.  This tree is ultrametric because all of the tips come up to the same timepoint (0 million years ago, i.e. now).

However, I can't make "don't use non-ultrametric trees" an absolute rule, because these days some of us have phylogenies that are tip-dated with fossil tips in the tree.  These trees are time-scaled, but they are not ultrametric.  Such trees are fine for BioGeoBEARS.

I put up this section since I keep seeing people just running their non-dated RaXML trees or whatever, which indicates severe misunderstandings...

> Any input on this is greatly appreciated - I don't want to end up in the "mistakes in the literature" section of the biogeobears website! :)
>

A good idea!

messages.body_plain:
---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Nick Matzke <mat...@nimbios.org>
Date: Mon, Jan 15, 2018 at 8:51 AM
Subject: Re: inquiry about using BioGeoBEARS
To: XXX

Hi XXX! Glad you are using the program!

Regarding the reviewer's comments [XXX about “sympatric range-copying cladogenesis” being the wrong term for single-area speciation events (e.g. A->A,A).

XXX

I wonder how the reviewer "knows" that sympatric speciation is impossible, since some researchers support the idea, but to each their own.  Any discussion of "sympatry" and "allopatry" must be relative to some scale of analysis, and what is sympatric at a coarse scale might be allopatric at a finer scale.  The term you have used seems fine to me, but if you want to avoid the fight, just say "within-area speciation" or something like that.  It is true that the method doesn't tell you anything about what happened at scales finer than your areas.

See e.g.:

Phylogenetic Methods in Biogeography
Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics

Vol. 42:441-464 (Volume publication date December 2011)
First published online as a Review in Advance on August 29, 2011
https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-ecolsys-102209-144710

Figure 4:

And Matzke (2013), Figure 1:

Matzke, Nicholas Joseph (2013). Probabilistic historical biogeography: new models for founder-event speciation, imperfect detection, and fossils allow improved accuracy and model-testing

What you are referring to as “sympatric range-copying cladogenesis” can also be called e.g. "narrow sympatry" (meaning within a single area, as opposed to broad sympatry) (Matzke 2013), "Duplication (within-area diversification)" (Ronquist and Sanmartin 2011), etc.

Cheers!
Nick

Nick
